sources.name: Pharmacology for Nurses: Glucocorticoids and Mineralocorticoids
sources.text: Synthetic glucocorticoids—such as prednisone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone—are commonly used in medicine to treat conditions such as asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Although glucocorticoids can be effective at treating certain conditions, they can have significant toxic effects over time that limit use. Prednisone Prednisone is an intermediate-acting steroid medication and a synthetic form of cortisol used to reduce inflammation. Like prednisolone, it is used in the treatment of a variety of conditions including asthma, allergic reactions, rheumatic disorders, respiratory disorders, and certain types of cancer. Prednisone ( Deltasone ) Typical dose : 5–60 mg orally daily depending on the specific disease entity being treated. Betamethasone ( Celestone , Betaject ) Typical dose for injectable : 0.25–0.9 mg/day intravenously or intramuscularly.

sources.name: Pharmacology for Nurses: Corticosteroids
sources.text: Prednisone ( Deltasone , Prednicot , Sterapred ) Initial dose: 5–60 mg orally daily in single dose or as 2–4 divided doses. Maintenance dosage is given daily or every other day (immediate release only). Table 25.9 is a drug prototype table for corticosteroids featuring prednisone. It lists drug class, mechanism of action, adult dosage, indications, therapeutic effects, drug and food interactions, adverse effects, and contraindications. Table 25.9 Drug Prototype Table: Prednisone (source: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/ ) Nursing Implications The nurse should do the following for clients who are taking corticosteroid drugs: Assess for hypersensitivity. Monitor blood pressure, sleep patterns, and potassium levels.
